rationale: Resolving the open necessary gap d82592dffc9d4a5893fbc6028fc438e7-gap-2 by checking the library's own documentation rather than reasoning about intent. doc.go's MsgProp contract describes a leader that appends entries to its log and broadcasts them when MsgProp reaches its Step method, and a follower that stores the message with the sender's ID and forwards it to the leader; no part of that contract conditions acceptance on the sender's membership, and nothing in node.go, doc.go or README assigns proposer authorization to the library. The only membership-based filtering the facade performs is for response messages from peers absent from Progress, and the proposal-channel block for a removed node is a local convenience whose own comment concedes it is unsound. That answers the gap in favour of caller-owned authorization, so the suspicion is refuted as a library defect while the measured behavior is retained as a fact with a narrow caller-facing caveat.

knowledge.statement: The documented MsgProp contract assigns no proposer-eligibility check to the library. doc.go states that when MsgProp is passed to the leader's Step method the leader first calls appendEntry to append entries to its log and then broadcasts them, that MsgProp is dropped by a candidate, and that on a follower it is stored with the sender's ID and later forwarded to the leader; the contract is about redirection of proposals, not about authorizing the proposer. Consistently, the checked-in handlers do not consult membership for proposals: stepFollower forwards MsgProp to r.lead, and stepLeader's MsgProp case checks only whether the leader itself is still a member. The Node facade does block its own proposal channel when it applies a config change that removes it, but that is a local best-effort whose accompanying comment calls it unsound and notes that the channel is reset on a leader change.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the Node and RawNode APIs in this snapshot, including a mixed cluster: the leader cannot in general verify the sender's identity beyond the self-declared From field, and the documented contract does not ask it to. Eligibility of voters and commit quorums still use the configuration; only proposer eligibility is unguarded.

d82592dffc9d4a5893fbc6028fc438e7-gap-2.explanation: The contract places sender eligibility on the caller. doc.go's MsgProp description (lines 305-316) defines the behaviour as a leader appending the entries it receives and a follower storing them with the sender's ID to forward onward, with no membership condition; neither node.go, doc.go nor README states or implies that the library authorizes a proposer, and the facade's only membership-based filtering is for response messages from ids absent from Progress. The removed-node proposal block in node.run is therefore a local best-effort convenience (its own comment says the logic is unsound and that the channel is reset when the leader changes), not a documented guarantee the leader-change path breaks.

knowledge.assertion: the documented MsgProp contract has no proposer-eligibility requirement; the handlers match it
the facade re-enables the proposal channel on any leader change and neither the forward nor the leader append path checks sender membership

interpretations.rationale: Resolution of the earlier conditional account. What changed: I stopped treating node.go's comment as the contract and read what the library actually documents. doc.go:305-316 describes MsgProp as a redirection mechanism - the leader appends entries to its log and broadcasts them, a candidate drops them, and a follower stores them with the sender's ID for forwarding - with no eligibility condition anywhere, and no statement in doc.go, node.go or README assigns proposer authorization to the library. That is decisive for the gap, because the question was which of the two readings the library promises: the documented behaviour is exactly what the probe measured, so the leader accepting a proposal whose sender is no longer in the configuration is the contract working as written, not a defect, and the whole suspicion is refuted. The behaviour gathered earlier remains valid and is retained as facts: the facade re-enables the proposal channel on any observed leader change regardless of membership (node.go:366-380), the removal branch that nils the channel is accompanied by a comment calling the logic unsound (node.go:400-432), stepFollower forwards MsgProp to r.lead without a membership test (raft.go:1720-1730), and stepping a MsgProp with From=3 into a leader whose configuration had just removed node 3 was accepted with no error and appended one entry (focused probe, native feedback only, no retained receipt). Counterevidence and boundaries: (a) the caller-authorization reading is supported not only by the silence of the contract but by DisableProposalForwarding, which exists so an operator can stop followers forwarding at all, treating forwarding as normal member behaviour; (b) RawNode users bypass the facade and can step any MsgProp, which is consistent with authorization being theirs; (c) the one caller-facing consequence I keep, without calling it a library defect, is that an application which infers membership from Propose failing will be misled after the next leader change, because the channel is silently re-enabled - that is a documentation-and-usage caveat, and the code comment already flags it; (d) the probe did not exercise the facade goroutine, so the facade half is a source reading, which is enough given the contract question is what mattered. No severity or safety consequence is claimed; nothing here bears on voter eligibility or commit quorums.
limitations: The facade half (proposal channel re-enabled on leader change) is a source reading, not an observation from a live Node goroutine driven through removal followed by a leader change.
The probe described here was native feedback without a retained receipt, so no check id or parsed indices are cited for it.
The refutation is contract-based: it establishes that the library does not promise proposer authorization, not that every application treats proposal acceptance as safe.
Downstream usage (etcd) was not examined, so no claim is made about how applications actually authorize proposers.
